feedback: Correct answer to anchor to: the flea does not have stronger muscles than a whole person; a person's muscles are far more powerful in total. Being very small and light makes extreme feats possible relative to body size — a tiny body weighs very little, so its muscles and springy parts fling it a huge distance compared to its own length.
If a learner takes the record literally ('the flea is just stronger'), ask who could actually move a brick and name the two different claims: strongest FOR ITS SIZE versus strongest OVERALL.

If a learner thinks a person-sized flea would still jump 150 times its body length, discuss that weight grows much faster than strength when you scale up (qualitatively, not with precise multipliers), so the giant version could not do it.
activities.intendedInsight: The record is a ratio, not a total; being small and light is the reason the feat is huge per body-length. Scaled up, the body would weigh far more (weight grows faster than strength), so the feat could not be repeated — the feat depends on being tiny.
learnerActions: Discuss the diagnostic question: a flea jumps about 150 times its body length, but a person cannot jump anywhere near 150 times their height — does that mean a flea has stronger muscles than a person? Explain what is really going on.
Argue whether a flea blown up to human size would still jump 150 times its body length, and why.
Give an example that separates 'strongest for its size' from 'strongest of all' — e.g. who could actually move a heavy brick, the person or the insect?
activities.title: Would a giant flea still win? Reasoning about scaling
